text: Selling through a wholesaler or larger buyer can give a Preah Vihear farmer access to larger markets, and this is particularly relevant for rice, cassava, cashew, mango, vegetables, and native chicken — commodities explicitly targeted by Cambodia's Agricultural Value Chain Competitiveness and Safety Enhancement Project (ACSEP) in Preah Vihear and neighboring provinces. A larger buyer may require minimum quantity, consistent quality, grading, packaging, moisture level, or a delivery schedule, so a higher quoted price can still mean a worse net return once transport, loading, packaging, grading, and rejected produce are subtracted. Farming systems in Rovieng district, Preah Vihear, are described as mainly rice-based with substantial diversification into other crops and livestock, and most paddy areas depend heavily on rainfall — Cambodia's national agricultural census found the average holding is about 1.7 hectares, with nearly 44% of holdings below 1 hectare and only about 20.6% using any irrigation, which is why aggregation with neighboring farmers often matters more than individual volume. During the wet season (roughly May–October), muddy roads, delayed harvesting, and difficulty drying grain affect transactions; during the dry season (roughly November–April), limited water and higher temperatures constrain production, particularly for irrigated crops. The relevant question is not "who pays the highest price" but "who gives the best realistic net return for my quantity, quality, location, transport, and payment needs" — the best buyer may be a local collector, a larger trader reached through aggregation, a cooperative, a processor, or a local market, and no single channel is universally best. No specific current Preah Vihear price, buyer, minimum quantity, or crop variety should be presented as fact without verification.
